Graphic Design & Prepress

Turning flat art into physical displays.

Three years at US Display Group, a corrugated POP display manufacturer — officially a Graphic Designer, unofficially the extra man who touched every stage of the process: art, dielines, prepress, printing, and cutting.

2D→3DFlat art to physical display

US Display Group designs and manufactures corrugated POP (point-of-purchase) displays — the branded cardboard fixtures you see anchoring end caps and checkout lines in retail stores. My title was Graphic Designer, but the job was never that narrow.

I became the extra man of the prototype pipeline — the person who could step into whatever stage needed help. That meant building art directly onto engineering dielines, running prepress checks, operating the flatbed printer, cutting prototypes on a large-format cutting machine, and building 3D renderings so clients could see a display before it existed.

It was a different kind of design job — one where the work didn't stop at the file export. A design only succeeded if it also folded, glued, and stood up correctly on a retail floor.

“My title said Graphic Designer. My day-to-day said art, prepress, printing, and cutting — whatever the prototype needed next.”

One project that shows the whole pipeline start to finish: a permanent floor display for Assets by Spanx — designed, laid out on the dieline, and rendered by me before it ever hit a flatbed printer or a cutting table.

Client

Assets by Spanx — "Love Your Assets"

1

Start with the header art

Every display starts as flat artwork — the illustrated figure, logo lockup, and product photography built as a standalone graphic before it ever touches a structural template.

2

Fit the art to the dieline

Here's the part most designers never touch: mapping that same artwork onto the engineering dieline — working around fold lines, glue tabs, and slot cuts so the graphic survives being folded into a physical object.

3

Repeat it panel by panel

A display is built from many panels, not one — shelves, risers, base units. Each one gets the same treatment: art built to the exact cut-and-fold geometry of that piece.

The finished 3D render

Built to show the client exactly how it would look on the floor — before a single panel was printed or cut.
